opus-5.5.text:
I think the right way to view it is as a new kind of tool. It's a very powerful one, and it's going to change how some parts of the work get done, but I don't think it replaces what mathematicians are actually trying to do.

When we worked on getting models to solve competition-level problems, like IMO problems, one thing that became clear is that problem-solving is only one piece of mathematics. A lot of what mathematicians care about is deciding which questions are worth asking. They build up concepts and frameworks, and they develop understanding. A proof that something is true is valuable, but the reason the community cares is often the insight it gives you into why it's true and what else that opens up.

So I'm optimistic that these models can become really good collaborators. You can imagine a mathematician working on a research program who has a bunch of lemmas they believe are true but that would take weeks to grind through. A model could help check those, or find counterexamples quickly, or point to a connection with some area of the literature they weren't aware of. That frees people up to spend more of their time on the creative, big-picture parts.

There's also an opportunity to make mathematics more accessible. A student who is stuck could have something like a tireless tutor that can engage with their reasoning, rather than just handing them an answer.

I'd also say that mathematicians should be involved in shaping this. They're the ones who know what good mathematics looks like, what rigor means, and what would actually be useful. The best outcomes will come from people in the field engaging with these tools, pushing on them, and telling us where they fall short. That's how we'll get systems that genuinely advance mathematics rather than just producing answers.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians build concepts and frameworks and seek understanding of why results are true, beyond solving competition problems.

r002.rationale: It describes AI helping check lemmas, find counterexamples, and surface connections, but does not propose using AI to accelerate development of new mathematical theories.

r003.rationale: It says AI could free mathematicians to focus on creative work, but does not discuss more capable coding AI increasing how much people work by expanding what they can attempt.

r004.rationale: It proposes AI as a collaborator but does not suggest exploring ideas in parallel by assigning different ideas to different models.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's a genuinely new situation, and I'd encourage mathematicians to hold two things at once.

The first is that the pace is real. When we were working on the IMO effort, the thing that surprised me most wasn't that a model could solve competition problems, it was how quickly the quality of the reasoning changed. A year earlier, you'd get something that looked like a proof but fell apart on inspection. By the time we were evaluating, the proofs were the kind of thing a grader could actually read, check line by line, and award full marks to. That trajectory doesn't stop at competition problems. Competitions are a convenient benchmark because the answers are known, but the underlying capability is reasoning for a long time about a hard problem without losing the thread, and that's exactly what research mathematics requires.

The second thing, though, is that I don't think this makes mathematicians obsolete, and I'd push back on anyone who frames it that way. Problem-solving is one part of mathematics. Deciding what's worth proving, building the right definitions, noticing that two areas are secretly the same, developing taste about which conjectures matter: those are the parts that have always been hardest to teach, and they're the parts where I'd be most cautious about claiming models are close. The IMO is, in a sense, the easy case, because someone else already chose the problem.

So my suggestion is to treat these systems the way you'd treat an extremely fast, somewhat strange collaborator. Use them to try the lemma you suspect is true but don't want to spend a week on. Use them to find the counterexample you'd otherwise miss. And expect that the frontier of what they can do will keep moving, so the question to keep asking is not "can it do my job," but "what becomes possible when checking a hard idea is cheap." I think the mathematicians who lean into that will end up doing more interesting mathematics, not less.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes problem-solving from choosing worthwhile questions, creating definitions, and connecting areas, but does not identify understanding mathematical structure as a central aim.

r002.rationale: It suggests using AI to try lemmas and find counterexamples, but does not propose using AI to accelerate the development of new mathematical theories.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss coding AI or explain that it could increase how much people work by expanding what they can attempt.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose exploring ideas in parallel by assigning different ideas to different AI models.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot to be excited about. Solving problems is a big part of mathematics, but so is figuring out which questions are worth asking, finding the right definitions, and understanding why something is true. If AI gets very good at solving problems, that could give mathematicians much more room to explore those other parts.

You might have an idea that would take weeks to test, and now you could get feedback much faster. That changes how adventurous you can be. You can try things that you otherwise wouldn’t have had time to pursue.

Of course, it would be a big change, and I think it’s reasonable to feel some uncertainty about it. But I’d encourage mathematicians to experiment with these tools and help shape how they’re used. A proof answers a question; there’s still a lot of work in turning that answer into understanding.

r001.rationale: The response presents understanding why a result is true, alongside choosing questions and definitions, as mathematical work beyond solving problems.

r002.rationale: It says AI could speed feedback and let mathematicians try more ideas, but does not propose using AI to develop new mathematical theories.

r003.rationale: It says AI could expand what mathematicians can attempt, but does not identify coding AI as the capability enabling that change.

r004.rationale: It does not propose exploring ideas in parallel or assigning different ideas to different AI models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematicians should be excited about it. There’s a lot more to mathematics than solving a problem once someone has handed it to you. A big part of the work is figuring out which questions are worth asking, finding useful definitions, and understanding how different ideas fit together.

If AI becomes very good at solving problems, that could let us explore much more freely. You could try an idea, work through examples, and see where it leads without spending months on every technical obstacle. That doesn’t make those technical achievements less valuable, but it could change where we put our effort.

Of course, it’s understandable to find that prospect unsettling, especially if solving hard problems is something you’ve invested a lot of yourself in. But I’d hope we can approach it with curiosity. The opportunity is to understand more mathematics, and to ask questions we wouldn’t have been able to approach before.

r001.rationale: It says mathematics includes understanding how different ideas fit together, beyond solving a handed problem.

r002.rationale: It suggests exploring ideas more freely, but does not clearly propose accelerating the development of new mathematical theories.

r003.rationale: It discusses trying ideas and overcoming technical obstacles, but does not mention coding AI or increased human work through expanded attempts.

r004.rationale: It does not propose assigning different mathematical ideas to different AI models for parallel exploration.
